Q: What is the difference between the switch and match syntax? A:

Python language does not have a traditional switch statement; instead, it uses match-case (introduced in Python 3.10), which is more powerful because it supports structural pattern matching with lists, tuples, dictionaries, and objects, unlike switch which mainly checks simple values.

  1. switch is a traditional conditional statement used in languages like Java and C++ to compare simple values such as numbers or strings.

  2. match-case in Python is an advanced pattern matching feature that can handle complex data types like lists, tuples, dictionaries, and objects without needing break statements.

    python`

    choice = "add"

match choice:
    case "add":
        print("Adding")

    case "delete":
        print("Deleting")

    case "update":
        print("Updating")

    case _:
        print("Invalid")

  3. case _ is the default case.

Q: Append tailwind classes on React Data Table's column headers A:

Generally in React, you can only style a child component in three ways:

  1. it accepts className / slot class props

  2. it accepts style objects / theme overrides

  3. you own the source and can change the actual markup

So for a datatable like this, the answer depends on the component you’re using. If it only accepts customStyles as JS style objects, then Tailwind utility classes won’t help much unless the library explicitly lets you pass class names down to the header cells.

That’s one reason modern frontend has moved much more toward source ownership in 2026 — very much the shadcn/ui model:

  • ship working primitives

  • let developers own the code

  • let them modify real markup and Tailwind classes directly

For tables, that’s especially useful because header styling is often just the start. Teams usually also want to change spacing, resize handles, row density, hover states, sticky columns, filter affordances, etc.

If you want a datatable that embraces that model, react-datatable is a good example. It’s source-owned, Tailwind-based, and meant to be modified in-place rather than themed from the outside only.

So instead of asking “how do I inject Tailwind classes into this abstraction?”, the more modern answer is often: use a table where you can just edit the source and change the classes directly.

Docs: why react-datatable

Q: React Data Table Lazy Loading or Pagination Loading A:

I would separate data loading from virtualization here, because they solve different problems.

  • pagination / infinite loading = how you fetch data from the API

  • virtualization = how many already-loaded rows you mount in the DOM

For 10k+ records, I would not fetch everything up front and then paginate client-side. I’d switch to server-backed pagination (or infinite loading), and only request the current window.

That’s exactly how I’d approach it with react-datatable:

  • choose online mode when the server should stay authoritative

  • choose pagination or infinite based on the UX

  • add virtualization separately if the loaded window itself gets heavy

The react-datatable docs actually explain this distinction pretty well and include examples for pagination and infinite scroll:

  • choose a data mode

  • tune virtualization

Q: How to install all required PHP extensions for Laravel? A:

Laravel 13 required PHP 8.3 - PHP 8.5 extensions (completed)

  • php: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) language interpreter.
  • php-fpm: PHP FastCGI Process Manager.
  • php-cli: Command-line interface for PHP.
  • php-common: Common files for PHP.
  • php-mysql: MySQL database integration for PHP.
  • php-zip: ZIP archive support for PHP.
  • php-gd: GD extension for PHP (image processing).
  • php-mbstring: Multibyte string support for PHP.
  • php-curl: cURL extension for PHP (URL transfers).
  • php-xml: XML support for PHP.
  • php-bcmath: Arbitrary precision mathematics extension for PHP.
  • openssl: OpenSSL toolkit (used by PHP for encryption).
  • php-tokenizer: Tokenizer support for PHP (used for parsing PHP code).
  • php-intl: This is frequently required by Laravel's internal helpers and many third-party packages for translation and localization.
  • php-sqlite3: The default testing suite in most Laravel applications.

These extensions will cover 99% of common php usage.

update and upgrade:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

add repository:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:ondrej/php

update repository:

sudo apt update

Newest version of php:

The complete list of all the needed PHP extensions:

sudo apt-get install -y php php-cli php-common php-fpm php-mysql php-zip php-gd php-mbstring php-curl php-xml php-bcmath openssl php-tokenizer php-intl php-sqlite3

If you want php extension for the specific version of PHP:

The complete list of all the needed PHP extensions with version 8.5 for Laravel 11:

sudo apt-get install -y php8.5 php8.5-cli php8.5-common php8.5-fpm php8.5-mysql php8.5-zip php8.5-gd php8.5-mbstring php8.5-curl php8.5-xml php8.5-bcmath openssl php8.5-tokenizer php8.5-intl php8.5-sqlite3

you can replace 8.5 with the version that you want (8.4, 8.3, 8.2, 8.1, 8.0, 7.4, ...).

Different versions of PHP for different versions of Laravel:

if you want to have different version of Laravel, you need different version of PHP, and you can have it with php-fpm

Run queue jobs or cronjobs:

For running queue jobs automatically, you need to have php-cli and run it with cronjob or supervisor.

To change the default php you can use this command:

sudo update-alternatives --config php

Q: Reusable components (Datatable) in React applications? A:

This is how I would do it with react-datatable:

I would keep the datatable itself reusable, and pass the page-specific parts in as configuration:

  • columns

  • data or query

  • getRowId

  • row actions / bulk actions

  • toolbar behavior

  • selection / preview / filters

So instead of copying EmployeeDatatable, SalaryDatatable, etc., I’d keep one table system and let each page define its own column model and behavior.

A simplified local example looks like this:

import { Datatable, type DatatableColumn } from "./react-datatable"

type Employee = {
  id: string
  name: string
  department: string
  status: "Active" | "Inactive"
}

const employeeColumns: DatatableColumn<Employee>[] = [
  {
    id: "name",
    header: "Name",
    accessorKey: "name",
    enableSorting: true,
    enableFiltering: true,
    filterType: "text",
  },
  {
    id: "department",
    header: "Department",
    accessorKey: "department",
    enableSorting: true,
    enableFiltering: true,
    filterType: "text",
  },
  {
    id: "status",
    header: "Status",
    accessorKey: "status",
    enableSorting: true,
    enableFiltering: true,
    filterType: "text-list",
    filterOptions: {
      options: [
        { label: "Active", value: "Active" },
        { label: "Inactive", value: "Inactive" },
      ],
    },
  },
]

export function EmployeeList({ rows }: { rows: Employee[] }) {
  return (
    <Datatable
      data={rows}
      columns={employeeColumns}
      getRowId={(row) => row.id}
      toolbar={{
        quickSearch: { placeholder: "Search employees..." },
        filterButton: true,
        displayOptions: true,
      }}
      selection={{ enabled: true }}
      rowActions={{
        onOpenRow: ({ row }) => {
          console.log("open employee", row.id)
        },
      }}
    />
  )
}

Then for another page, you keep the same Datatable but swap:

  • the row type

  • the columns

  • the actions

  • optionally the loading mode

That scales much better than cloning a table component per page.

The main architectural point is: reuse the table engine, customize the table definition.

There is a full example here:
local data example

And if you want the setup path behind it:
get started with react-datatable

Shorter version if you want it more Stack Overflow-ish:

This is how I would do it with react-datatable:

  • keep one reusable Datatable

  • pass columns, data/query, and handlers from each page

  • let each page define its own row model and actions

  • don’t clone the whole table component per screen unless the UI is genuinely a different product surface

That gives you reuse without collapsing everything into one rigid component.

Q: Resolve conflicts using remote changes when pulling from Git remote A:

If you truly want to discard the commits you've made locally, i.e. never have them in the history again, you're not asking how to pull - pull means merge, and you don't need to merge. All you need do is this:

# fetch from the default remote, origin
git fetch
# reset your current branch (main) to origin's main
git reset --hard origin/main

I'd personally recommend creating a backup branch at your current HEAD first, so that if you realize this was a bad idea, you haven't lost track of it.

If on the other hand, you want to keep those commits and make it look as though you merged with origin, and cause the merge to keep the versions from origin only, you can use the ours merge strategy:

# fetch from the default remote, origin
git fetch
# create a branch at your current master
git branch old-master
# reset to origin's master
git reset --hard origin/master
# merge your old master, keeping "our" (origin/master's) content
git merge -s ours old-master
